description: Online team (Montreal) for Be An Earth System Trend Detective! We are building a web tool that lets anyone pick NASA Earth science variables (temperature, precipitation, vegetation...), see how they change over time and across regions, and test whether the trends are statistically significant. Led by a data analyst (Python, statistics, forecasting, Tableau, web dashboards). Looking for: Earth science, data/statistics, front-end. EN/FR.
summary:
Scars from Space investigates one change everyone suspects and few have tested: did the full-scale invasion of February 2022 change how Ukraine burns? We counted 1.6 million NASA FIRMS fire detections (MODIS 2001–2025, VIIRS 2012–2025) across Ukraine's 25 regions. For each region we predicted the expected number of fires from its own pre-war history and that month's weather (MERRA-2 via NASA POWER).

Across Ukraine as a whole, 2022 shows no clear spike. Region by region, the country split: frontline regions burned 2.2–2.7 times more than rear regions relative to expectation, on both satellites and in every model version (p ≤ 0.0003). Kherson region recorded 24,544 detections against 12,047 expected, yet a standard Mann-Kendall trend test reports "no trend" there. Sudden, human-caused breaks need break-aware methods.

The approach supports environmental damage accounting and recovery planning, and it works for any sudden change seen from orbit. All results are region-level totals for past months only.
details:
What it does. Scars from Space answers the challenge's four questions for Ukraine since February 2022. What changed: vegetation-fire activity seen by NASA satellites. Where: region by region, on a map and a ranked chart. How much: observed fires divided by the fires that weather and history predict. Is it significant: tested against each region's own pre-war variability, with a correction for testing 25 regions at once.
How it works. (1) Download NASA FIRMS standard fire archives for Ukraine: MODIS Collection 6.1 (2001–2025) and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m (2012–2025), 1.94 million raw detections. (2) Keep presumed vegetation fires only (FIRMS type 0) and drop low-confidence detections: 1.6 million remain. (3) Count detections per region and month inside Ukraine's internationally recognised borders. (4) Average MERRA-2 weather from NASA POWER over each region (maximum temperature, precipitation, humidity, topsoil wetness) as monthly anomalies. (5) Model each region separately: log fires ~ month of year + long-term trend + weather anomalies, fitted on pre-war months; pre-war years are predicted leave-one-year-out. (6) Test post-war against pre-war residuals (Welch t-test, Benjamini–Hochberg correction) and compare frontline with rear regions (Mann–Whitney). (7) Cross-examine: rerun without the trend term and on the second satellite. MODIS and VIIRS are never added together.
Findings. Nationally, 2022 is not a spike. Frontline regions burned 2.2–2.7 times more than rear regions relative to expectation, in all four model and satellite versions (p ≤ 0.0003). The two satellites agree on which regions changed most (Spearman ρ = 0.84). Kherson is the only region significant on both satellites (VIIRS 2.6×, q = 0.007; MODIS 1.65×, q = 0.04). Ten of 15 rear regions burned significantly less than expected.
Fire energy and a visible break. With summed fire radiative power instead of counts, the frontline–rear contrast grows to 3.2–3.7 times (p ≤ 0.0003), and Kherson reaches 4.6 times its expected fire energy (q = 0.004). NASA MODIS true-color imagery shows the Kakhovka reservoir draining within 17 days of the dam's destruction on 6 June 2023: a sudden break of the kind our method targets. We do not convert fire energy into CO2, because fire duration is unknown from a few satellite passes a day.
Acute vs chronic. As a contrast, we queried the NASA FIRMS VIIRS 2020 archive for Lebanon. Within 3 km of the 4 August 2020 Beirut port explosion, VIIRS recorded one fire detection (2.8 MW) about 8.5 hours after the blast, and only one other in all of 2020 (a separate port fire on 10 September). A one-second shock needs a different witness: NASA JPL's ARIA team mapped Beirut's damage with Sentinel-1 radar. Beirut was an industrial disaster, not a war; it shows the other end of the time scale.
Benefits and impact. It turns raw fire pixels into a defensible yes, no or not proven for each region, and shows why a plain trend test misses sudden breaks. Since 30 September 2026 the Register of Damage for Ukraine (Council of Europe) accepts the State of Ukraine's claims for environmental damage, and the Initiative on GHG Accounting of War has to separate war fires from ordinary fires when it estimates the climate cost of the war. Our open, weather-adjusted regional baseline makes that split in a way anyone can rerun and check. Regions that burned far above expectation, such as Kherson, are natural places to start surveying burned steppe, forest and farmland for recovery. The pipeline is reusable for any dated shock: dam failures, industrial disasters, burning bans or extreme wildfire seasons in Canada.
Limits we state openly. A fire detection is heat seen from orbit, not a strike. We do not claim why rear regions burned less. The aging MODIS satellites drift in orbit, so VIIRS is the main witness. Only region-level totals for past months are published: no coordinates and no near-real-time data.
Tools. Python (pandas, geopandas, shapely, pyogrio, numpy, scipy, pymannkendall, matplotlib, Pillow, requests, remotezip); HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website, hosted on Netlify. All scripts and data files are published on the website. AI disclosure: code, charts and texts were drafted with an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) under the team's direction; this is marked in every script header, on every chart and on the website.
